newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW--US factory output off 0.5 pct in Oct.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW--US factory output off 0.5 pct in Oct.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Federal Reserve said industrial production fell 0.5 percent in October down from a revised 0.3 percent rise the prior month.
Meanwhile, capacity utilization stood at 82.7 percent in the month compared to a revised reading of 83.4 in September.
Experts had expected an unchanged reading on output and capacity use at 83.0 percent.
JOHN LONSKI, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MOODY'S: "What we're looking at here is a pullback in manufacturing activity."
"I'm struck by the across-the-board weakness in this report on industrial production."
Lonski was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.

CHERYL KATZ, SENIOR ECONOMIST, MERRILL LYNCH & CO INC: "Obviously, the number came in a little bit better (for the Treasury market) than expectations. A lot of it had to do with the decline in manufacturing productivity, which had to do with the (General Motors) strike. With capacity utilization remaining where it is, there obviously are no bottleneck pressures at the manufacturing level."
TIM MCGEE, CHIEF ECONOMIST, TOKAI BANK LTD: "The number was weaker than expected. The General Motors strike had a big effect on auto production.

"Outside of autos, things dipped a little bit. It mainly shows that after the production spurt we had in response to the strong consumer earlier this year, production has started to slow down as a result of the consumer slowing back down
"This is the way to keep inventories under control."
DANA JOHNSON, HEAD OF RESEARCH, FIRST CHICAGO CAPITAL MARKETS: "It's definitely softer than I expected."

Johnson continued: "And it's not all attributable to the GM strike. Ex-autos, manufacturing was still down a tenth of a percent. There's pretty widespread softeness in the industrial sector and it goes beyond the GM strike.
"It's on the bullish side for the fixed-income market because it certainly adds to the evidence that the industrial sector is pretty mediocre right now.
"Fundamentally, manufacturing is not doing much, even when you extract the effects from the strike," he added.

KEVIN FLANAGAN VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "I don't know how far the (Treasury) market can really take (the report); they may embrace it for the most part as somewhat favorable news, but it really has a lot to do with the problems at General Motors. Nevertheless, a negative figure of this magnitude and the fact that capacity was down 0.7 percent will probably be viewed as somewhat favorable. It doesn't change the Fed outlook or anything else. We'll have to wait another month before we get a good read on manufacturing ... chances are next month's report will just be a make-up or a rebound because the (GM) strike is over."
ELLIOTT PLATT, DIRECTOR OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH, DONALDSON, LUFKIN & JENRETTE SECURITIES CORP: "(The report) is one more piece of evidence regarding the economy slowing down.
"The numbers suggest business probably is expecting weak retail demand, weak plant equipment spending, and they're cutting back production in order to make sure there's excess build-up in inventory.
"This certainly fits a scenario of what I think is going to (equate to) 1.3 percent (Gross Domestic Product) growth this quarter ... Ex-auto the numbers would still be down 0.1 percent," Platt added.

ROBERT BRUSCA, CHIEF ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "This is a strike-contaminated number. We've had four, five months in a row of manufacturing output increases, so if you take out autos, you only have a slight slide.
"You can't get too excited about this. What we'll see is a bounce back and stronger data next month as automakers try and catch up on output," he added.
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
